label: Conditional Probability
overview: Conditional probability P(A|B) answers: given that B already happened, how likely is A? On the SAT this almost always comes from a two-way frequency table where you restrict your universe to one row or column, then count within that restricted group. The key is identifying which condition limits your sample space.

keyFormulas.name: From a table
keyFormulas.latex: P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\text{count in both A and B}}{\text{count in B (row or column total)}}

workedExamples.problem: A survey of 200 students asked whether they play a sport and whether they have a part-time job. 80 play a sport, of whom 24 also have a job. What is the probability that a randomly selected student has a job, given that they play a sport?

steps.title: Identify the condition
steps.content: 'Given that they play a sport' means we restrict our universe to the 80 sport-players only.

steps.title: Apply the formula
steps.content: Among sport-players (80), 24 also have a job.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the grand total as the denominator instead of the row/column total
commonMistakes.fix: The denominator in P(A|B) is always the total count for the given condition B, not the overall table total.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reversing the condition: computing P(A|B) when the question asks for P(B|A)
commonMistakes.fix: Read the 'given' clause carefully. 'Given that they play a sport' means sport is in the denominator.

quickTip: Circle or highlight the 'given' row or column — that row's (or column's) total becomes your denominator, and you count only within that highlighted section.
